title: Mirror After One Deletion
statement:
You get a string s of lowercase letters. You may delete at most one character from it (or none).

Return true if the result can read the same forwards and backwards, otherwise false.

examples.why: Delete the c to get "abba". The outer a's match, then b and c clash, and only dropping the right one of the two works.
Two letters are out of place: the middle "xcy" needs two deletions.
It already reads the same both ways, so no deletion is needed.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
hints: Compare the outer pair of characters, then move inward. While they match, nothing is wrong yet.
At the first mismatch, one of those two characters must be the one you delete. Which two candidates are left to check?
At the first mismatch at positions i and j, return whether s[i+1..j] or s[i..j−1] reads the same both ways. Check both: the first one that looks fine is not always right.

explain.intuition:
Walk two pointers in from the ends. As long as the characters match, those pairs are fine whatever you delete later, so skip them. At the first mismatch, one of the two clashing characters has to go, because otherwise this pair stays broken. That leaves exactly two candidates.

So check both: is the inner part without the left character a palindrome, or the inner part without the right character? Each check is one more linear scan with no deletions left. You must try both. In "abbca" dropping the left b leaves "bc", which fails, while dropping the right c leaves "bb".
steps: While i < j and s[i] === s[j], move both inward.
Otherwise return isMirror(i + 1, j) || isMirror(i, j − 1), where isMirror checks a range with no deletions allowed.
pitfalls: Trying only one side at the mismatch, such as always skipping the left character. "abbca" needs the right one dropped.
Allowing a second skip inside the follow-up checks. After the one deletion, the rest must match exactly.
Building new substrings for every check in a loop. Pass indexes instead, so each check costs O(n) with no copying.

solutions.title: Try every deletion
solutions.idea: Check the string itself, then the string with each single position removed.

solutions.title: Two pointers, branch once
solutions.idea: Match from both ends. At the first mismatch, check whether skipping the left or the right character leaves a palindrome.

followups: Allow up to k deletions. Why does branching at every mismatch blow up, and what does a DP over (i, j) give you?
Return which index to delete (or −1 if none is needed). Which one do you report when both work?
